terms: what is snap called in wyoming
supplements.citation: Wyoming DFS SNAP consumer page (dfs.wyo.gov); DFS SNAP and POWER Policy Manual Section 401 (Application/Intake Process)
supplements.heading: Wyoming's public brand is plain "SNAP," and it is applied for via a PAPER application only — this pack found no online self-service SNAP application portal, a genuine structural contrast with most other states in this roster
supplements.text: Wyoming DFS's live consumer-facing materials use only the generic federal name "SNAP" (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) — this pack found no distinctive Wyoming-specific program nickname the way California has "CalFresh" or Washington has "Basic Food." Unlike most other states this pack's roster has built, Wyoming's SNAP application process is explicitly PAPER-ONLY: DFS's own consumer page states plainly "Wyoming SNAP is applied for via a paper application," available in English (DFS 100) and Spanish (DFS 100S), and submitted to a local DFS office in person, by mail, by fax, or by email to snappowerservice@wyo.gov. This pack searched specifically for an online self-service portal comparable to Delaware's ASSIST or California's BenefitsCal and found none for Wyoming — a genuine structural fact worth disclosing rather than a research gap, since DFS's own site routes every application channel (mail, fax, email, in-person) back to the same paper DFS 100 form rather than any online intake system. Wyoming's SNAP program is administered directly and centrally by DFS through its Field Offices — a state-administered program with no county-level policy authority, structurally similar to this roster's Delaware, Nebraska, Connecticut, North Carolina, Ohio, New Jersey, Tennessee, Indiana, Missouri, Maryland, Colorado, South Carolina, Alabama, Louisiana, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Utah, Iowa, Arkansas, Mississippi, Kansas, and New Mexico packs. Wyoming also runs POWER (Personal Opportunities with Employment Responsibilities), its TANF-funded cash-assistance program, administered by the same agency and referenced throughout the same combined policy manual.

supplements.citation: Wyoming DFS Table I: SNAP Income Limits (published for 10/1/2025-9/30/2026); DFS SNAP and POWER Policy Manual Section 502 (Categorically Eligible Persons); Section 800 (Asset Limits); USDA SNAP State Options Report, 16th Ed. (Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility, p.24)
supplements.heading: STRUCTURAL FLAGSHIP FINDING, confirmed by both a primary state source and a primary federal source: Wyoming is one of only 9 states nationally WITHOUT Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility — its categorical-eligibility gate is narrow SSI/POWER/Tribal-TANF recipiency, not a 200% FPL income screen
supplements.text: Wyoming DFS's own current Table I: SNAP Income Limits table (published for October 1, 2025 - September 30, 2026) lists three gross/net income columns by household size, with NO 200% FPL column at all: a 165% FPL gross-income test used for the elderly/disabled separate-household provision ($2,152 for household size 1, $4,421 for size 4), the underlying 130% FPL standard gross-income limit that most households must meet ($1,696 for size 1, $3,483 for size 4), and the 100% FPL net-income limit that applies to all households ($1,305 for size 1, $2,680 for size 4). This pack found and independently cross-checked, via USDA FNS/FNA's own 16th-edition SNAP State Options Report (June 2024), that Wyoming is listed under "No BBCE (9)" for the Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility option — one of only nine states nationally (alongside Alaska, Arkansas, Kansas, Mississippi, Missouri, South Dakota, Tennessee, and Utah, per the same source) that has NOT adopted the BBCE option letting states align SNAP's asset and gross-income limits with a state's own TANF noncash-benefit program. Wyoming DFS's own manual independently confirms this: Section 502 defines categorical eligibility narrowly — an assistance unit is categorically eligible ONLY when all members are receiving POWER (Wyoming's TANF cash program), Tribal TANF, and/or SSI, with no 200% FPL income-based categorical-eligibility gate anywhere in the manual. This pack reads this as a genuine minority-position structural fact, not an error or omission: a Wyoming household that is NOT receiving POWER/Tribal TANF/SSI faces BOTH the 130%/100% FPL income tests AND the real $3,000/$4,500 resource limit described below — there is no broader income-based shortcut around the resource test the way most other states in this roster (via BBCE) provide for the large majority of their SNAP households. Per Section 800, the resource limit is $3,000 for assistance units where no member is 60+ or disabled, and $4,500 for assistance units with a member 60+ years old or disabled — this figure matches the current federal FY2026 COLA-adjusted resource-limit floor under 7 CFR 273.8(a) exactly, a genuine confirmed-current contrast with this roster's Delaware pack, whose DSSM text was found below the federal floor. Vehicles receive an unusually generous exemption given Wyoming's narrow categorical-eligibility structure: Section 800's vehicle-asset subsection exempts ALL licensed and unlicensed vehicles used for transportation from any fair-market-value or equity-value test — no per-vehicle dollar threshold or count limit this pack could find, a genuinely favorable provision for a state without BBCE's blanket vehicle exemption via categorical eligibility.

supplements.citation: USDA SNAP State Options Report, 16th Ed. (Drug Felony Disqualifications, p.17, Wyoming under 'No disqualification'); DFS SNAP and POWER Policy Manual Section 610 (Fleeing Felons/Probation or Parole Violator)
supplements.heading: FLAGSHIP FINDING (primary-source correction of a widely-repeated, template-style secondary-source claim): Wyoming has FULLY opted out of the federal drug-felony SNAP ban — several secondary sources describing a 'modified' ban conditioned on sentence/treatment compliance are wrong, not merely stale
supplements.text: 21 U.S.C. § 862a(a)(2) sets a federal default: anyone convicted of a state or federal felony for possessing, using, or distributing a controlled substance after August 22, 1996 is permanently ineligible for SNAP unless a state opts out or modifies the ban under § 862a(d)(1). This pack found the SAME near-verbatim claim repeated across several low-quality SNAP-aggregator/secondary sources describing Wyoming as having a 'modified' drug-felony ban conditioned on compliance with the terms of a sentence, including supervision and substance-abuse-treatment requirements — language this pack could trace to NO identifiable Wyoming-specific primary source (statute, regulation, or DFS manual section) anywhere. This pack instead fetched USDA FNS/FNA's own 16th-edition SNAP State Options Report directly and found Wyoming listed plainly under "No disqualification (28)" for the Drug Felony Disqualifications option (7 CFR 273.11(m)) — the same category as, e.g., Delaware, Illinois, and Utah. This pack independently corroborated that finding against Wyoming's own DFS SNAP and POWER Policy Manual: the 600-series section range (601 Age through 610 Fleeing Felons/Probation or Parole Violator) contains NO drug-felony-conviction disqualification section at all — the ONLY criminal-justice-related disqualification category in Wyoming's entire manual is fleeing-felon/probation-or-parole-violator status (Section 610), which requires all four of: an outstanding felony warrant, and one of three specific law-enforcement-notification conditions (an agency states intent to enforce/arrest within 20 days of a state's information request, presents a felony arrest warrant, or states intent within 30 days of a specific request) — a narrower, differently-scoped provision from a drug-felony ban entirely. This pack's reading: Wyoming has FULLY opted out of the federal drug-felony SNAP ban, not merely modified it, and the 'modified ban' secondary-source claim this pack found repeated is simply incorrect for Wyoming, not merely dated — a stronger correction than a typical staleness catch, since this pack found no evidence such a provision ever existed in Wyoming's own regulatory history the way Delaware's now-repealed DSSM 2027 did.

supplements.citation: Wyoming DFS Table I: SNAP Income Limits (FFY2026, 10/1/2025-9/30/2026); USDA SNAP State Options Report, 16th Ed. (Standard Medical Deduction Project, p.27, Wyoming under 'SMD')
supplements.heading: DISCLOSED INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY: Wyoming DFS's own "Do I Qualify" consumer page carries stale standard-deduction and shelter-cap dollar figures that do NOT match DFS's own current Table I page for the same FFY2026 cycle
supplements.text: Wyoming DFS's current Table I page (self-dated "October 1, 2025 - September 30, 2026") confirms the following FFY2026 deduction figures directly: a Standard Deduction of $209 for assistance-unit (AU) sizes 1-3, $223 for AU size 4, $261 for AU size 5, and $299 for AU size 6 and above; a Standard Medical Deduction of $175 for deductions in excess of $35/month (Wyoming participates in USDA's Standard Medical Deduction Project per the 16th-edition State Options Report, a demonstration option letting elderly/disabled households claim this flat figure in lieu of itemizing actual medical costs above $35, with the option to itemize instead if actual costs exceed $175); a maximum excess-shelter-cost deduction of $744 for nonelderly/nondisabled assistance units (uncapped for households with an elderly or disabled member, per standard federal SNAP rules); a utilities-only standard of $340 (two non-heating/cooling utilities); Wyoming's Standard Utility Allowance (SUA, for households with heating/cooling costs) of $510; a telephone-only allowance of $57; a Homeless Shelter Deduction of $198.99 (matching the current national FY2026 federal maximum homeless-shelter-deduction figure exactly); and the standard 20% earned-income deduction. This pack separately fetched DFS's own "SNAP: Do I Qualify?" consumer page and found it states a DIFFERENT, materially lower set of figures for the identical categories: a Standard Deduction of $177 (AU 1-3), $184 (AU 4), $215 (AU 5), $246 (AU 6+), and a $569 maximum shelter deduction for nonelderly/nondisabled households — both sets of figures this pack could not date-stamp to a specific prior FFY cycle with certainty, but which plainly do not match the current, explicitly-dated Table I figures for the same FFY2026 period. This pack treats the Table I page (which self-dates its figures directly against a visible historical FFY2025 table on the same page) as authoritative over the "Do I Qualify" page's undated, apparently-stale figures, and flags this specific internal DFS-site inconsistency explicitly rather than silently picking one number — a finding structurally similar to, though independently discovered from, this roster's Delaware pack's internal-DSSM-staleness catches.

supplements.citation: DFS SNAP and POWER Policy Manual Section 708 (ABAWD Requirements); USDA FNA SNAP Time Limit (ABAWD) Waivers FY2025-2029 index (Wyoming absent from the state-response list)
supplements.heading: Wyoming currently has NO area-wide ABAWD waiver anywhere in the state — it does not appear at all on USDA's FY2025/FY2026 waiver-response list; Wyoming's own manual already reflects the current post-OBBBA age band and explicitly exempts Indian tribal members from the ABAWD time limit
supplements.text: An able-bodied adult without dependents (ABAWD) is limited to three countable months of SNAP within a 36-month period absent 80 hours/month of a qualifying work activity or an exemption. Wyoming DFS's own manual Section 708 defines an ABAWD as someone able-bodied, ages 18 through 64 as of the OBBBA's July 4, 2025 effective date, in an assistance unit without a dependent under age 14 — this pack confirms Wyoming's own regulatory text is ALREADY current with the post-OBBBA age band (unlike this roster's Delaware pack, whose DSSM text was found lagging behind the live consumer page on this exact point). Wyoming operates on a fixed 36-month tracking period rather than a rolling one, with the current fixed period running October 1, 2024 - September 30, 2027. Section 708(B) lists seven categories exempt from the ABAWD benefit limit: under 18 or over 65 (as of 7/4/2025); medically certified as physically/mentally unfit for employment; parent of a household member under 14; residing in an assistance unit with a member under 14; otherwise exempt from work requirements (other than solely for being over 60); pregnant; OR a member of an Indian tribe — this last exemption is directly relevant given Wyoming's Wind River Reservation population (shared by the Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho tribes, spanning Fremont and Hot Springs Counties). This pack separately fetched USDA FNA's SNAP Time Limit (ABAWD) Waivers FY2025-2029 state-response index directly and found Wyoming does not appear ANYWHERE on the list — not among states with an FY2025 waiver, an FY2026 waiver, a denial, or a termination — meaning Wyoming has not requested (and DFS's own manual does not describe) any area-specific unemployment-based ABAWD waiver for the current period. This pack's reading: Wyoming currently enforces the ABAWD work-requirement time limit statewide with no waived area, a genuinely different posture from many other states in this roster that carry at least a partial-area waiver.

supplements.citation: Wyoming DFS SNAP consumer pages (no RMP mentioned anywhere in fetched materials); WebSearch corroboration (secondary)
supplements.heading: Wyoming does NOT operate a Restaurant Meals Program
supplements.text: The Restaurant Meals Program (RMP) is a state OPTION under 7 CFR § 274.7(g) letting elderly (60+), disabled, and homeless SNAP recipients buy prepared, hot meals from authorized restaurants with EBT year-round. This pack found no mention of an RMP anywhere in DFS's live consumer materials or in any of the nine SNAP and POWER Policy Manual accordion sections this pack fetched, and found consistent secondary-source corroboration that Wyoming does not currently operate one. This pack found no pending Wyoming legislation that would establish one. Wyoming's operative answer for an applicant asking whether they can use SNAP at a restaurant is a plain no — EBT purchases are limited to grocery-style items intended for home preparation. This pack separately confirms, per the food-restriction-waiver finding below, that Wyoming's SNAP-eligible-item list is about to become MORE restrictive rather than less (excluding sweetened, carbonated beverages effective 2/1/2027), a direction opposite to an RMP expansion.

terms: what can i buy with snap
supplements.citation: USDA FNA, Wyoming SNAP Food Restriction Waiver Demonstration Project approval letter (dated 3/4/2026, effective 2/1/2027)
supplements.heading: NOT YET IN EFFECT AS OF THIS PACK'S FETCH DATE: Wyoming has an approved, 2-year federal demonstration-project waiver to exclude "sweetened, carbonated beverages" statewide from SNAP-eligible food, starting February 1, 2027
supplements.text: This pack fetched a primary USDA FNA approval letter, dated March 4, 2026 and addressed to Wyoming's Governor and DFS Director, confirming FNS/FNA approved a Wyoming DFS request (formally submitted January 7, 2026) to operate a 'novel demonstration project' under Section 17(b)(1)(B) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, amending SNAP's statutory definition of 'food' to exclude 'sweetened, carbonated beverages' from items purchasable with SNAP benefits statewide. The approval is for 2 years, EFFECTIVE FEBRUARY 1, 2027 — meaning that as of this pack's own fetch/verification date (2026-08-12), the restriction is approved but NOT YET IN EFFECT; SNAP recipients in Wyoming can still purchase sweetened, carbonated beverages with EBT as of this pack's fetch. The approval letter states explicitly this Project applies to 100% of the Wyoming SNAP caseload with NO household opt-out permitted, and that FNS/FNA will evaluate the Project's impact via quarterly reports. This pack found this waiver as part of a broader wave of similar state-specific SNAP soda/candy exclusion demonstration waivers approved by USDA across multiple states in the 2025-2026 window (a policy direction this pack did not independently research beyond Wyoming's own specific approval letter). This is a genuinely time-sensitive fact: an applicant asking today what they can buy with SNAP in Wyoming should be told sweetened, carbonated beverages ARE currently purchasable, with an EXPLICIT flag that this changes on 2/1/2027.

terms: food distribution program on indian reservations
supplements.citation: DFS SNAP and POWER Policy Manual Section 402 (Client's Rights); Section 401 (Application/Intake); Section 708(B)(7) (ABAWD Indian-tribal-member exemption)
supplements.heading: SNAP and the Food Distribution Program on Indian Reservations (FDPIR) are mutually exclusive in Wyoming — a household must choose one program or the other, never both
supplements.text: This pack researched specifically, per this task's scope, whether Wyoming's DFS SNAP manual carries any state-specific notes on FDPIR interaction or reservation-specific administration, given Wyoming's Wind River Reservation (shared by the federally recognized Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho tribes, spanning Fremont and Hot Springs Counties). This pack found and confirms three specific, narrow points, and discloses that this is the full extent of what DFS's own fetched manual sections and consumer pages state — this pack found no broader Wyoming-specific tribal SNAP administration structure (e.g., no separate Tribal SNAP-administering entity analogous to some other states' tribal 638 SNAP agreements) and does not assume one exists beyond what is documented here. First: Section 402 (Client's Rights) states plainly that an applicant has the right to be informed of 'the choice of participating in either the Food Distribution Program on Indian Reservations (FDPIR) or the SNAP program prior to any benefits being authorized,' and that 'under no circumstances shall any household participate simultaneously in the SNAP and the Food Distribution Program' — a standard federal SNAP/FDPIR mutual-exclusion rule (households on a reservation where FDPIR operates may enroll in either program but not both at once), stated explicitly in Wyoming's own manual text. Second: Section 401 directs that an enrolled Tribal member who is a resident of Fremont or Hot Springs County (the two counties overlapping Wind River) and who is applying for the TRIBAL TANF program (not SNAP directly) may have that application processed at the appropriate Tribal TANF office rather than a standard DFS Field Office — this pack found no equivalent Tribal-office SNAP-application routing instruction, meaning SNAP applications themselves still route through standard DFS channels even for Wind River residents, while Tribal TANF applications route separately. Third: per the ABAWD supplement above, Section 708(B)(7) exempts any 'member of an Indian tribe' from the ABAWD work-requirement time limit entirely, regardless of residence on or off a reservation — this is a categorical membership-based exemption, not geographically restricted to Wind River specifically.

supplements.citation: DFS SNAP and POWER Policy Manual Section 1201 (Establishing a SNAP Certification Period)
supplements.heading: Wyoming caps ALL SNAP certification periods at 12 months, with NO extended 24-month track even for all-elderly/disabled no-earned-income households
supplements.text: Section 1201(D)(1) states plainly that Wyoming certification periods are based on calendar months and 'never [exceed] 12 months.' This pack specifically checked whether Wyoming carries the extended 24-month certification track several other states in this roster provide for all-elderly/disabled no-earned-income households (as this roster's Delaware pack does, at DSSM 9068.2) and found the opposite: Section 1201(J) states explicitly that, effective January 1, 2016, 'the maximum certification period allowed is 12 months for households in which ALL adult members are elderly or disabled and have NO EARNED income, provided other circumstances appear stable' — meaning the 12-month cap in Wyoming applies uniformly, with no longer track available for any household type. Certification periods may be shortened only in narrow circumstances (correcting an error, or increasing up to the 12-month maximum when an expedited household later provides required verification), and once set generally may not be changed mid-period.
